steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on jointly calibrating the spatial and temporal parameters between a camera and a global pose sensor such as a motion capture system. Motivate the problem, review target-based and target-less calibration, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motion capture systems and why camera / global pose sensor calibration matters
2. Example: target tracking / automatic labeling
3. Target-based calibration methods and their limits
4. Why online target-less calibration is needed
5. Online target-less calibration in VINS; observability and degenerate motion
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motion capture
   - widely used for 6DoF pose tracking; high accuracy (sub-millimeter)
   - odometry / SLAM datasets use it for ground truth pose
   - collection platform of one dataset, passive markers (Fig. 1(a))
   - potential in computer vision beyond localization not fully exploited
   - key: spatial-temporal calibration params of camera and global pose sensor (Fig. 1(b))
2. Example (Fig. 2(b))
   - target tracking or automatic labeling task with motion capture
   - camera frame rigidly linked with marker frame tracked by mocap
   - target = point f; mocap gives position of f and pose of marker frame
   - with calibration params -> image coordinates of f automatically via rigid body link
3. Target-based methods
   - two categories: target-based vs target-less
   - target-based more accurate (prior knowledge of calibration target); widely used in multi-sensor calibration
   - target-based spatial-temporal hand-eye calibration first presented in earlier work
   - aligns mocap trajectory with camera trajectory from PnP with target; intrinsics fixed
   - accuracy limited by PnP on every image; raw pixel measurements discarded after PnP
   - isolated processing misses correlation raw pixels <-> mocap measurements
   - ours (target-based): uses all raw sensor data, optimizes spatial-temporal params, intrinsics and trajectory together
4. Limits -> online
   - offline, non-real-time only; lots of manual effort
   - markers on camera may be removed during experiments -> spatial param changes
   - temporal param changes too: different clocks, transmission delays, data jam, jitter, skew
   - online target-less calibration worth exploiting: saves effort, easier to apply
5. VINS
   - online target-less calibration popular in visual-inertial navigation systems (VINS)
   - EKF-based methods most popular (computational efficiency)
   - sufficient motion excitation -> VINS spatial-temporal params observable
   - specific motion profiles -> some DoF of calibration params unobservable
   - identify + avoid degenerate motion
6. Contributions
   - first to calibrate spatial-temporal params of camera + global pose sensor together, from raw monocular pixels + global pose measurements
   - two novel approaches: target-based and target-less
   - observability analysis for target-less method; degenerate motions -> partial params unobservable
   - degenerate motions verified in simulation; accuracy + consistency on hand-held real-world datasets
   - online calibration of time-varying params with target-less method

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Today motion capture systems are used a lot for 6DoF pose tracking because they are very accurate (sub-millimeter). In odometry and SLAM research most datasets use them to provide the ground truth pose. Fig. 1(a) shows the collection platform from one of these datasets, which has some passive markers of the kind that are typically used with motion capture systems. But apart from localization methods, the potential of motion capture systems in computer vision has not been fully used. The key to this is the spatial-temporal calibration parameters of the camera and the global pose sensor (see Fig. 1(b)).

For example, in Fig. 2(b) we assume a target tracking or automatic labeling task that is done with the motion capture system. The camera \left\{C\right\} is rigidly linked with the marker frame \left\{M\right\} that the motion capture system tracks. The target is regarded as a point f. The motion capture system gives {}^{G}{p_{f}} and \left\{{\begin{array}[]{*{20}{c}}{{}_{M}^{G}q}&{{}^{G}{p_{M}}}\end{array}}\right\}. If we have the spatial-temporal calibration parameters that link \left\{M\right\} and \left\{C\right\}, then the image coordinates of f can be obtained automatically through the rigid body link (f\to G\to M\to C).

This example shows why it is useful to have a spatial-temporal calibration between a camera and a global pose sensor. In the literature, methods for spatial-temporal calibration are split into two categories, target-based methods and target-less methods. Target-based methods are more accurate than target-less methods, because they benefit from prior knowledge of the calibration target. Target-based methods are widely used in multi-sensor calibration tasks. Target-based spatial-temporal hand-eye calibration was first presented in earlier work. There, the spatial-temporal parameters are calibrated by aligning the motion capture trajectory with the camera trajectory, and the camera trajectory is obtained with the calibration target by the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm. The camera intrinsic parameters are assumed to be fixed. So the accuracy of that method is limited by the PnP algorithm, which is used on every single image. After PnP all the raw pixel measurements are thrown away. Because the motion capture sequence and the camera sequence are processed in isolation, the inherent correlation between the raw pixel measurements and the motion capture measurements can not be uncovered. Our target-based calibration algorithm is different, it fully uses all the raw sensor data and optimizes the spatial-temporal parameters, the camera intrinsics and the trajectory at the same time.

[limits of these methods -> online]
- offline, non-real-time only; lots of manual effort
- markers may be removed during experiments -> spatial parameter changes
- temporal parameter changes: different clocks, transmission delays, data jam, jitter, skew
- online target-less calibration worth exploiting: saves effort, easier to apply

[VINS]
- online target-less calibration popular in visual-inertial navigation systems (VINS); EKF-based most popular (efficiency)
- sufficient motion excitation -> spatial-temporal params observable
- specific motion profiles -> some DoF unobservable; need to identify + avoid degenerate motion

[contributions]
- first joint spatial-temporal calibration of camera + global pose sensor from raw monocular pixels + global pose
- two novel approaches: target-based, target-less
- observability analysis for target-less; degenerate motions making partial params unobservable
- simulation check of degenerate motions; accuracy + consistency on hand-held real-world datasets
- online calibration of time-varying params (target-less)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Today motion capture systems are used a lot for 6DoF pose tracking because they are very accurate (sub-millimeter). In odometry and SLAM research most datasets use them to provide the ground truth pose. Fig. 1(a) shows the collection platform from one of these datasets, which has some passive markers of the kind that are typically used with motion capture systems. But apart from localization methods, the potential of motion capture systems in computer vision has not been fully used. The key to this is the spatial-temporal calibration parameters of the camera and the global pose sensor (see Fig. 1(b)).

For example, in Fig. 2(b) we assume a target tracking or automatic labeling task that is done with the motion capture system. The camera \left\{C\right\} is rigidly linked with the marker frame \left\{M\right\} that the motion capture system tracks. The target is regarded as a point f. The motion capture system gives {}^{G}{p_{f}} and \left\{{\begin{array}[]{*{20}{c}}{{}_{M}^{G}q}&{{}^{G}{p_{M}}}\end{array}}\right\}. If we have the spatial-temporal calibration parameters that link \left\{M\right\} and \left\{C\right\}, then the image coordinates of f can be obtained automatically through the rigid body link (f\to G\to M\to C).

This example shows why it is useful to have a spatial-temporal calibration between a camera and a global pose sensor. In the literature, methods for spatial-temporal calibration are split into two categories, target-based methods and target-less methods. Target-based methods are more accurate than target-less methods, because they benefit from prior knowledge of the calibration target. Target-based methods are widely used in multi-sensor calibration tasks. Target-based spatial-temporal hand-eye calibration was first presented in earlier work. There, the spatial-temporal parameters are calibrated by aligning the motion capture trajectory with the camera trajectory, and the camera trajectory is obtained with the calibration target by the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm. The camera intrinsic parameters are assumed to be fixed. So the accuracy of that method is limited by the PnP algorithm, which is used on every single image. After PnP all the raw pixel measurements are thrown away. Because the motion capture sequence and the camera sequence are processed in isolation, the inherent correlation between the raw pixel measurements and the motion capture measurements can not be uncovered. Our target-based calibration algorithm is different, it fully uses all the raw sensor data and optimizes the spatial-temporal parameters, the camera intrinsics and the trajectory at the same time.

But these methods are only suitable for offline calibration that is not real-time, and they need a lot of manual effort. The markers attached to the camera may be removed during experiments, and this changes the spatial calibration parameter. The temporal calibration parameter would also change, because of different clocks, transmission delays, data jam, jitter, and skew. So an online target-less calibration method is also worth exploiting, since it saves human effort and makes it easier to apply.

In recent years online target-less calibration has gotten a lot of attention in visual-inertial navigation systems (VINS). Among these, EKF-based methods are the most popular because they are computationally efficient. One of these works pointed out that the spatial-temporal calibration parameters of VINS are observable if there is sufficient motion excitation. But under specific motion profiles some degrees of freedom of the calibration parameters would be unobservable. It is crucial to identify possible motion degradation, and to avoid such motion, in order to apply these kinds of algorithms reliably.

The contributions of this work are:

- As far as we know, this is the first work that calibrates the spatial-temporal parameters of the camera and the global pose sensor simultaneously, using raw monocular camera pixel measurements and global pose measurements.

- We propose two new approaches to estimate the spatial-temporal parameters, one target-based and one target-less.

- We give a detailed observability analysis for the target-less calibration method we propose and we identify the degenerate motions that can happen in practice and make part of the calibration parameters unobservable.

- We verify the degenerate motions in simulation and we evaluate the accuracy and consistency of the two proposed algorithms on hand-held real-world datasets.

- We show that the target-less method can be applied to online calibration of time-varying spatial-temporal parameters.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Nowadays, motion capture systems are widely used to perform 6DoF pose tracking thanks to their high accuracy (sub-millimeter). In odometry and SLAM research, most datasets use them to provide the ground truth pose [1,2,3]. The collection platform from [2] shown in Fig. 1(a) displays some passive markers typically associated with motion capture systems. Apart from its application to localization methods, the potential of motion capture systems in computer vision has not been fully exploited. The key is the spatial-temporal calibration parameters of the camera and the global pose sensor (see Fig. 1(b)).

For instance, in Fig. 2(b), we assume a target tracking or automatic labeling task performed with the motion capture system. The camera \left\{C\right\} is rigidly linked with the marker frame \left\{M\right\} tracked by the motion capture system. The target is regarded as a point f. The motion capture system provides {}^{G}{p_{f}} and \left\{{\begin{array}[]{*{20}{c}}{{}_{M}^{G}q}&{{}^{G}{p_{M}}}\end{array}}\right\}. Given the spatial-temporal calibration parameters linking \left\{M\right\} and \left\{C\right\}, the image coordinates of f can be obtained automatically via the rigid body link (f\to G\to M\to C).

This example illustrates the benefits of a spatial-temporal calibration between a camera and a global pose sensor. In the literature, methods for spatial-temporal calibration are divided into two categories: target-based methods and target-less methods. Target-based methods are more accurate than target-less methods, benefiting from prior knowledge of the calibration target, and are widely used in multi-sensor calibration tasks [4,5,6]. Target-based spatial-temporal hand-eye calibration was first presented in [7]. The spatial-temporal parameters are calibrated by aligning the motion capture trajectory with the camera trajectory, which is obtained with the calibration target by the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm. The camera’s intrinsic parameters are assumed to be fixed. Therefore, the accuracy of [7] is limited by the PnP algorithm employed on every single image, and after the PnP process all raw pixel measurements are discarded. Processing the motion capture sequence and the camera sequence in isolation cannot uncover the inherent correlation between raw pixel measurements and motion capture measurements. In contrast, our target-based calibration algorithm fully uses all the raw sensor data to optimize the spatial-temporal parameters, camera intrinsics and trajectory simultaneously.

However, these methods are only suitable for offline, non-real-time calibration and require significant manual effort. Markers attached to the camera may be removed during experiments, changing the spatial calibration parameter. Moreover, the temporal calibration parameter would also change due to different clocks, transmission delays, data jam, jitter, and skew [8]. Therefore, an online target-less calibration method is also worth exploiting, saving human effort and making it easier to apply.

In recent years, online target-less calibration has attracted significant attention in visual-inertial navigation systems (VINS) [9,10,11]. Among these, EKF-based methods are the most popular thanks to their computational efficiency. [9] pointed out that, given sufficient motion excitation, the spatial-temporal calibration parameters of VINS are observable. However, under specific motion profiles, some degrees of freedom of the calibration parameters would be unobservable [12]. Identifying potential motion degradation, and avoiding such motion, is crucial to applying these algorithms reliably.

The contributions of this work are summarized as:

- • To our knowledge, this is the first work to simultaneously calibrate the spatial-temporal parameters of the camera and the global pose sensor, with raw monocular camera pixel measurements and global pose measurements.

- • We propose two novel approaches to estimate the spatial-temporal parameters, considering both target-based and target-less methods.

- • We provide a detailed observability analysis for the proposed target-less calibration method and identify the degenerate motions that may occur in practice, making part of the calibration parameters unobservable.

- • We verify the degenerate motions in simulation and evaluate the accuracy and consistency of the two proposed algorithms with hand-held real-world datasets.

- • We demonstrate the applicability of the target-less method to online calibration of time-varying spatial-temporal parameters.
